claim: Prior studies suggest that clinical trials are often hampered by problems in design, conduct, and reporting that limit their uptake in clinical practice.
source: Prior studies suggest that clinical trials are often hampered by problems in design, conduct, and reporting that limit their uptake in clinical practice.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research in the field, as indicated by the statement's context in the abstract.

claim: The proportion of clinical trials fulfilling four conditions of informativeness (importance of the clinical question, trial design, feasibility, and reporting of results) was 26.4% (95% CI 18.9–35.0).
source: The proportion meeting four conditions for informativeness was 26.4% (95% CI 18.9–35.0).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data from the study's primary outcome analysis.

claim: Sixty-seven percent of participants were enrolled in informative trials.
source: Sixty-seven percent of participants were enrolled in informative trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of participant enrollment across the trial cohort.

claim: The proportion of informative trials did not differ significantly between the three disease areas (ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and lung cancer).
source: The proportion of informative trials did not differ significantly between our three disease areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing proportions across disease areas.

claim: The majority of randomized interventional trials designed to guide clinical practice possess features that may compromise their ability to do so.
source: Our results suggest that the majority of randomized interventional trials designed to guide clinical practice possess features that may compromise their ability to do so.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the finding that 73.6% of trials did not meet all four conditions of informativeness.

claim: A substantial proportion of clinical trials aimed at informing clinical practice are marred by flaws in design, execution, analysis, and reporting.
source: Numerous analyses suggest that a substantial proportion of clinical trials aimed at informing clinical practice are marred by flaws in design, execution, analysis, and reporting (Chalmers et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2014; Fergusson et al., 2005; Glasziou et al., 2014; Ioannidis et al., 2014; Al-Shahi Salman et al., 2014; Yordanov et al., 2018; Yordanov et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: The initial research response to COVID-19 illustrated that existing oversight mechanisms fail to prevent the initiation of flawed trials.
source: The initial research response to COVID-19 illustrated the fact that existing oversight mechanisms fail to prevent the initiation of flawed trials (Bugin and Woodcock, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study about COVID-19 research.

claim: Trials that have features rendering them unlikely to inform clinical practice may do harm by misleading potential participants about their benefits and by diverting patient-participants from otherwise informative research efforts.
source: While unexpected events can stymie well-conceived and implemented studies, trials that have features rendering them unlikely to inform clinical practice may do harm by misleading potential participants about their benefits and by diverting patient-participants from otherwise informative research efforts (Zarin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about the potential harms of uninformative trials.

claim: Over half of the 125 interventional trials in the cohort were studies of drug or biologic interventions (77 trials; 61.6%).
source: Over half of the 125 interventional trials in our cohort were studies of drug or biologic interventions (77 trials; 61.6%).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by descriptive data from the trial cohort.

claim: The majority of trials were phase 2 (24 trials, 19.2%) or phase 3 trials (50 trials, 40.0%).
source: The majority were phase 2 (24 trials, 19.2%) or phase 3 trials (50 trials, 40.0%).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by descriptive data from the trial cohort.

claim: Trial status was 'completed' in 99 of 125 trials (79.2%) and 'terminated' in 15 trials (12.0%).
source: Trial status was 'completed' in 99 of 125 trials (79.2%) and 'terminated' in 15 trials (12.0%) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by descriptive data from the trial cohort presented in Table 1.

claim: Ninety-three trials (74.4%) were first registered on ClinicalTrials.gov prior to or within 30 days of the listed trial start date.
source: Ninety-three trials (74.4%) were first registered on ClinicalTrials.gov prior to or within 30 days of the listed trial start date.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by descriptive data from the trial cohort.

claim: A sensitivity analysis excluding the 35 trials in the lowest quartile for target enrollment resulted in a proportion of informative trials of 35.6% (95% CI 25.7–46.3).
source: As a sensitivity analysis, we re-analyzed our primary outcome excluding the 35 trials in the lowest quartile for target enrollment. This resulted in a proportion of informative trials of 35.6% (95% CI 25.7–46.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a sensitivity analysis performed by the authors.

claim: A sensitivity analysis excluding phase 1/2 and phase 2 trials resulted in 30.7% (95% CI 21.9–40.7) of trials meeting four conditions of informativeness.
source: We performed a second sensitivity analysis on our primary outcome excluding phase 1/2 and phase 2 trials. This resulted in 30.7% (95% CI 21.9–40.7) of trials meeting four conditions of informativeness.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a sensitivity analysis performed by the authors.

claim: A total of 193,839 participants were enrolled in the 125 trials in the cohort, of which 129,973 (67.1%) were enrolled in informative trials.
source: A total of 193,839 participants were enrolled in the 125 trials in our cohort, of which 129,973 (67.1%) were enrolled in informative trials.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of participant enrollment.

claim: The proportion of ischemic heart disease trials that was informative was 27.5% (95% CI 14.6–43.9).
source: The proportion of ischemic heart disease trials that was informative was 27.5% (95% CI 14.6–43.9)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis for the ischemic heart disease subgroup.

claim: The proportion of diabetes mellitus trials that was informative was 31.6% (95% CI 19.9–45.2).
source: the proportion for diabetes mellitus trials was 31.6% (95% CI 19.9–45.2)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis for the diabetes mellitus subgroup.

claim: The proportion of lung cancer trials that was informative was 14.3% (95% CI 4.0–32.7).
source: and the proportion for lung cancer was 14.3% (95% CI 4.0–32.7) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis for the lung cancer subgroup, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Proportions of informative trials did not vary significantly by disease area (p-value = 0.23).
source: Proportions did not vary significantly by disease area (p-value = 0.23) (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing disease areas, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Each surrogate measure contributed considerably to the stepwise decline in the proportion of informative trials.
source: Each surrogate measure contributed considerably to the stepwise decline in the proportion of informative trials (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Of the 35 trials not meeting the feasibility condition, 21 failed to reach 85% of planned patient enrollment.
source: Of the 35 trials not meeting our feasibility condition, 21 failed to reach 85% of planned patient enrollment (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of trials failing the feasibility condition.

claim: Of the nine trials not meeting the reporting condition, six were not subject to FDAAA 801 results reporting requirements.
source: Of the nine trials not meeting our reporting condition, six were not subject to FDAAA 801 (U.S. Public Law, 2007a) results reporting requirements (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of trials failing the reporting condition.

claim: Increased understanding of the importance of biomarker status in treatment response from trial initiation to completion rendered the results for a non-selected population less clinically relevant for trial NCT01104155.
source: For one trial (NCT01104155 – phase 2 study in non-small cell lung cancer investigating the combination of eribulin mesylate in combination with intermittent erlotinib), increased understanding of the importance of biomarker status in treatment response from trial initiation to completion rendered the results for a non-selected population less clinically relevant (Supplementary file 5; Mok et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study and represents an inference about why a trial was not incorporated into clinical synthesizing documents.

claim: Trial NCT00918138's primary outcome (change from baseline in 24-hr mean weighted glucose at week 4) did not meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in a high-quality systematic review investigating the same topic.
source: In another case, trial NCT00918138 investigated the addition of saxagliptin to extended-release metformin in adult patients with type 2 diabetes (Neutel et al., 2013). Its primary outcome, change from baseline in 24-hr mean weighted glucose at week 4, did not meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in a high-quality systematic review (SR) investigating the same topic (Men et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the trial publication and a systematic review, and represents an inference about why the trial was not included.

claim: Trial NCT00954707 sponsors submitted results to ClinicalTrials.gov but never published them, which may have hampered inclusion in a clinical synthesizing document.
source: In a third case, trial NCT00954707 (a phase 4 trial investigating duration of dual anti-platelet therapy in 2509 individuals undergoing placement of a Cypher cardiac drug eluting stent) sponsors submitted results to ClinicalTrials.gov but never published them. This may have hampered inclusion in a clinical synthesizing document.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of trial reporting behavior and speculation about its impact on inclusion in synthesizing documents.

claim: Out of the 18 trials not meeting the importance condition, 8 trials had no published primary outcome results.
source: Out of the 18 trials, 8 trials not meeting the importance condition had no published primary outcome results.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of trials failing the importance condition.

claim: The most common reasons for a high risk of bias score in the 30 trials not meeting the design condition were lack of blinding of participants and personnel, and lack of blinding of outcome assessment and selective reporting.
source: Finally, the most common reasons for a high risk of bias (ROB) score in the 30 trials not meeting our design condition were lack of blinding of participants and personnel, and lack of blinding of outcome assessment and selective reporting (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of risk of bias assessments.

claim: Studies sponsored by industry were significantly more likely to fulfill all four conditions of informativeness than those not sponsored by industry (50.0 vs. 6.0%, p-value <0.001).
source: Studies sponsored by industry were significantly more likely to fulfill all four conditions of informativeness than those not sponsored by industry (50.0 vs. 6.0%, p-value <0.001) (Table 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing industry-sponsored and non-industry-sponsored trials.

claim: There was a non-random association between trial phase and informativeness.
source: Using the two-sided Fisher's exact test, there was a non-random association between trial phase and informativeness, and type of intervention and informativeness (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using Fisher's exact test.

claim: There was a non-random association between type of intervention and informativeness.
source: Using the two-sided Fisher's exact test, there was a non-random association between trial phase and informativeness, and type of intervention and informativeness (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using Fisher's exact test.

claim: Just over one-fourth of trials demonstrated adequacy for study feasibility, reporting, importance, and design.
source: In our analysis, just over one-fourth of trials demonstrated adequacy for study feasibility, reporting, importance, and design.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the primary outcome data showing 26.4% of trials met all four conditions.

claim: 73.6% of trials contained a limitation in design, conduct, or reporting that compromised their ability to inform clinical decision-making.
source: The remaining 73.6% contained a limitation in design, conduct, or reporting that compromised their ability to inform clinical decision-making.
evidence: This claim is directly inferred from the primary outcome data showing 26.4% of trials met all four conditions.

claim: Certain shortcomings of clinical trials are a result of experimenting in a dynamic real-world environment and cannot be entirely avoided.
source: Certain shortcomings of clinical trials are a result of experimenting in a dynamic real-world environment and cannot be entirely avoided.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about the challenges of conducting clinical trials.

claim: Changes in medical practice may render a research question irrelevant to clinical practice.
source: For example, changes in medical practice may render a research question irrelevant to clinical practice
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about factors that can affect trial relevance.

claim: An emerging pandemic might lead to under-recruitment in clinical trials.
source: an emerging pandemic might lead to under-recruitment.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about factors that can affect trial recruitment.

claim: Increased oversight by research funders, including requirements for landscape analysis of completed and ongoing clinical trials to ensure trials are addressing important questions, and the provision of independent scientific review to highlight vulnerabilities in trial design, are measures that can be implemented to increase the likelihood that trials will be informative.
source: For example, increased oversight by research funders, including requirements for landscape analysis of completed and ongoing clinical trials to ensure trials are addressing important questions, and the provision of independent scientific review to highlight vulnerabilities in trial design (Bierer et al., 2018), are measures that can be implemented to increase the likelihood that trials will be informative.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a recommendation based on inference.

claim: Many methodological weaknesses in trial design can be corrected at minor cost.
source: Many methodological weaknesses in trial design can be corrected at minor cost (Yordanov et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Each condition of informativeness goes unfulfilled in roughly equal proportions.
source: Our study also demonstrated that each condition of informativeness goes unfulfilled in roughly equal proportions (Supplementary file 2), suggesting that vigilance is required throughout the life cycle of a trial.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Vigilance is required throughout the life cycle of a trial.
source: Our study also demonstrated that each condition of informativeness goes unfulfilled in roughly equal proportions (Supplementary file 2), suggesting that vigilance is required throughout the life cycle of a trial.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the finding that each condition of informativeness goes unfulfilled in roughly equal proportions.

claim: The study's estimates for the fraction of studies fulfilling criteria for recruitment feasibility are in line with prior studies.
source: Our estimates for the fraction of studies fulfilling criteria for recruitment feasibility are in line with prior studies (Carlisle et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2011; Korn et al., 2010; Walters et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research cited.

claim: The fraction of trials at low risk of bias is similar to prior estimates.
source: The fraction of trials at low ROB is similar to prior estimates (Yordanov et al., 2015; Ndounga Diakou et al., 2017; Vale et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research cited.

claim: The study's estimate for the fraction of studies fulfilling reporting requirements (90.0%) is in line with prior studies that evaluated both ClinicalTrials.gov results deposition and publication.
source: Our estimate for the fraction of studies fulfilling reporting requirements (90.0%) is in line with prior studies that evaluated both ClinicalTrials.gov results deposition and publication (Chen et al., 2016; Phillips et al., 2017), both of which were deemed acceptable means of results reporting in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research cited.

claim: This study is the first to apply the four conditions of informativeness jointly to a sample of trials, in addition to assessing importance via citation in clinical synthesizing documents.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to apply these conditions jointly to a sample of trials, in addition to assessing importance via citation in clinical synthesizing documents.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' assessment of the novelty of their study based on their knowledge of the literature.

claim: Many lung cancer trials were of early phase (46.4% phase 2) and did not meet design criteria due to lack of blinding.
source: Although there was no significant difference in informativeness observed between our three disease areas, many lung cancer trials were of early phase (46.4% phase 2) and did not meet design criteria due to lack of blinding (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of lung cancer trials.

claim: For some lung cancer trials, blinding may have been difficult to achieve but nonetheless would contribute to an elevated risk of bias.
source: We acknowledge that for some of these trials, blinding may have been difficult to achieve but nonetheless would contribute to an elevated ROB.
evidence: This claim represents an inference about the challenges of blinding in certain trial contexts.

claim: Trials were assessed as 'low risk of bias' if there was no or incomplete blinding, but the outcome was unlikely to be influenced by lack of blinding, as per the Cochrane risk of bias guidelines.
source: Of note, trials were assessed as 'low ROB' if there was no or incomplete blinding, but the outcome was unlikely to be influenced by lack of blinding, as per the Cochrane ROB guidelines (Higgins et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study, based on established guidelines.

claim: Phase 4 trials fared worse than phase 3 trials, with only 2 of 19 fulfilling all four conditions of informativeness.
source: Phase 4 trials fared worse than phase 3 trials, with only 2 of 19 fulfilling all four conditions of informativeness (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis comparing phase 3 and phase 4 trials.

claim: Prior research demonstrates greater recruitment challenges for non-industry funded trials.
source: This is in keeping with prior research demonstrating greater recruitment challenges for non-industry funded trials (Carlisle et al., 2015), in addition to diminished compliance with timely results reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov (DeVito et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prior research demonstrates diminished compliance with timely results reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov for non-industry funded trials.
source: This is in keeping with prior research demonstrating greater recruitment challenges for non-industry funded trials (Carlisle et al., 2015), in addition to diminished compliance with timely results reporting on ClinicalTrials.gov (DeVito et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Funding bodies and academic medical centers may not provide adequate resources for fulfilling the clinical mission of the trials they support.
source: These results suggest that funding bodies and academic medical centers may not provide adequate resources for fulfilling the clinical mission of the trials they support.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the finding that non-industry sponsored trials were less likely to be informative.

claim: Several recent initiatives aim at improving various aspects of informativeness, including increased consideration given to the importance and clinical relevance of the research question, the evidentiary basis for proposed research, study registration and reporting, by many funders.
source: Several recent initiatives aim at improving various aspects of informativeness, including increased consideration given to the importance and clinical relevance of the research question, the evidentiary basis for proposed research, study registration and reporting, by many funders (Moher et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research describing these initiatives.

claim: The implementation of new frameworks, such as INQUIRE, if widely adopted, may lead to further improvements in research quality.
source: The implementation of new frameworks, such as INQUIRE, developed to guide academic institutions in addressing waste in research, including assessments of research design, feasibility, transparency, relevance, and internal and external validity, if widely adopted, may lead to further improvements in research quality (von Niederhäusern et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents speculation about the potential impact of new frameworks.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has highlighted both the susceptibility of our clinical research enterprise to substandard trials, while also showing what is possible with robust research vetting, coordination, and collaboration.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has highlighted both the susceptibility of our clinical research enterprise to substandard trials, while also showing what is possible with robust research vetting, coordination, and collaboration (Kimmel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research about COVID-19 clinical trials.

claim: Scoring trial importance required citation in a clinical synthesizing document.
source: For example, scoring trial importance required citation in a clinical synthesizing document.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The measure of trial importance may have erroneously classified some informative trials as at risk of being uninformative (e.g. trials that evaluate disease management in niche populations that are not addressed in practice guidelines or systematic reviews).
source: This measure may have erroneously classified some informative trials as at risk of being uninformative (e.g. trials that evaluate disease management in niche populations that are not addressed in practice guidelines or SRs).
evidence: This claim represents the authors' acknowledgment of a potential limitation in their methodology.

claim: The measure of trial importance may have misclassified some trials as informative (e.g. trials addressing already resolved clinical hypotheses, which might nevertheless be cited in systematic reviews).
source: It may also have misclassified some trials as informative (e.g. trials addressing already resolved clinical hypotheses, which might nevertheless be cited in SRs).
evidence: This claim represents the authors' acknowledgment of a potential limitation in their methodology.

claim: None of the 18 trials not fulfilling the importance condition involved niche populations.
source: To the former, none of the 18 trials not fulfilling the importance condition involved niche populations (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data analysis of trials failing the importance condition.

claim: Some trials may inform clinical practice despite failing the study's criteria.
source: We also acknowledge that some trials may inform clinical practice despite failing our criteria.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' acknowledgment of a limitation in their approach.

claim: The DAPT Study (NCT00977938) was a large phase 4 study that was deemed at high risk of bias in several high-quality systematic reviews.
source: The DAPT Study (NCT00977938) was a large phase 4 study that was deemed at high ROB in several high-quality SRs (Xu et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to systematic reviews that assessed the DAPT Study.

claim: The DAPT Study has had an important impact on the clinical management of antiplatelet therapy following drug-eluting stent placement.
source: However, this study has had an important impact on the clinical management of antiplatelet therapy following drug-eluting stent placement (Cutlip and Nicolau, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing the impact of the DAPT Study.

claim: The study's metrics are best understood as capturing factors that seriously (but not necessarily fatally) compromise a trial's prospects of informing practice and that are rectifiable.
source: Our metrics are best understood as capturing factors that seriously (but not necessarily fatally) compromise a trial's prospects of informing practice and that are rectifiable.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' interpretation of what their metrics measure.

claim: The study applied strict inclusion/exclusion criteria when identifying the cohort of clinically directed randomized controlled trials, thus limiting generalizability to other types of trials.
source: Second, we applied strict inclusion/exclusion criteria when identifying our cohort of clinically directed randomized controlled trials, thus limiting generalizability to other types of trials, including those involving diagnostics, early phase trials, nonrandomized trials or interventions that do not advance to FDA approval.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' acknowledgment of a limitation in the generalizability of their findings.

claim: Other types of trials (including those involving diagnostics, early phase trials, nonrandomized trials or interventions that do not advance to FDA approval) would require different criteria for assessing informativeness, given their primary goal of informing regulatory or research decision-making.
source: The latter would require different criteria, given their primary goal of informing regulatory or research decision-making.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' inference about the need for different criteria for other trial types.

claim: Developing surrogate measures of informativeness for other types of trials represents an avenue for future research.
source: Developing surrogate measures of informativeness for other types of trials represents an avenue for future research.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' suggestion for future research directions.

claim: The study used a longitudinal and sequential approach, since some of the conditions were only relevant once others had been met.
source: Third, we used a longitudinal and sequential approach, since some of the conditions were only relevant once others had been met.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Incorporation into a clinical synthesizing document can only occur once results have been reported.
source: For example, incorporation into a clinical synthesizing document can only occur once results have been reported.
evidence: This claim represents a logical inference about the sequential nature of the conditions.

claim: The sequential approach enabled the study to address the primary outcome with an economy of resources.
source: Our sequential approach enabled us to address our primary outcome with an economy of resources.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' justification for their methodological approach.

claim: The study does not enable an assessment of the proportion of trials fulfilling three of the four criteria in isolation from each other.
source: However, our study does not enable an assessment of the proportion of trials fulfilling three of the four criteria in isolation from each other.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' acknowledgment of a limitation in their approach.

claim: Changes in research practices or policy occurring over the last decade might produce different estimates for the proportion of randomized trials that are informative.
source: In addition, changes in research practices or policy occurring over the last decade might produce different estimates for the proportion of randomized trials that are informative.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' speculation about how temporal changes might affect their findings.

claim: The study's evaluation is limited by the accuracy of information contained in the ClinicalTrials.gov registration record and in the published literature.
source: Fourth, our evaluation is limited by the accuracy of information contained in the ClinicalTrials.gov registration record and in the published literature.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' acknowledgment of a limitation in their data sources.

claim: The use of other sources of data, such as U.S. FDA regulatory documents, in addition to study protocols and statistical analysis plans uploaded onto ClinicalTrials.gov, could be considered for use in future evaluations of trial informativeness.
source: The use of other sources of data, such as U.S. FDA regulatory documents, in addition to study protocols and statistical analysis plans uploaded onto ClinicalTrials.gov, could be considered for use in future evaluations of trial informativeness.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' suggestion for future research improvements.

claim: There is broad agreement that uninformative trials exist.
source: Although there is broad agreement that uninformative trials exist, there is no clear consensus on methods to identify which trials are uninformative.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about the field.

claim: There is no clear consensus on methods to identify which trials are uninformative.
source: Although there is broad agreement that uninformative trials exist, there is no clear consensus on methods to identify which trials are uninformative.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about the field.

claim: The study's retrospective assessment is an initial step toward developing prospective criteria that can be used to highlight trials of concern, thereby enabling early corrective intervention.
source: Our retrospective assessment is an initial step toward developing prospective criteria that can be used to highlight trials of concern, thereby enabling early corrective intervention.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' interpretation of the significance of their work.

claim: Trial volunteers are generally told that their participation will advance clinical practice.
source: Trial volunteers are generally told that their participation will advance clinical practice.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about clinical trial informed consent practices.

claim: One-third (33%) of patient-participants in the study were enrolled in trials that possessed at least one feature that compromised their goal of informing clinical practice.
source: However, one-third (33%) of patient-participants in our study were enrolled in trials that possessed at least one feature that compromised their goal of informing clinical practice.
evidence: This claim is directly inferred from the finding that 67% of participants were enrolled in informative trials.

claim: Sponsors and investigators often face unforeseeable challenges.
source: Sponsors and investigators often face unforeseeable challenges, and trials with flaws in design and implementation occasionally uncover actionable insights.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about the challenges of conducting clinical trials.

claim: Trials with flaws in design and implementation occasionally uncover actionable insights.
source: Sponsors and investigators often face unforeseeable challenges, and trials with flaws in design and implementation occasionally uncover actionable insights.
evidence: This claim represents general knowledge about clinical trial outcomes.

claim: Research systems and oversight should address persistent barriers to fulfilling the societal mission of clinical research.
source: Nevertheless, research systems and oversight should address persistent barriers to fulfilling the societal mission of clinical research.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' recommendation based on their findings.

claim: The study created a cohort of randomized, interventional clinical trials in three broad disease areas that are representative of the clinical research enterprise and that have a significant impact on patient morbidity and mortality: ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and lung cancer.
source: We created a cohort of randomized, interventional clinical trials in three broad disease areas that are representative of the clinical research enterprise and that have a significant impact on patient morbidity and mortality: ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and lung cancer.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study restricted inclusion to trials that appeared to be aimed at informing clinical practice by selecting trials with a stated purpose of treatment or prevention of disease and with a primary clinical outcome or appropriate surrogate.
source: We restricted inclusion to trials that appeared to be aimed at informing clinical practice by selecting trials with a stated purpose of treatment or prevention of disease and with a primary clinical outcome or appropriate surrogate.

source: We established milestones that could serve as objectively verifiable surrogates for four conditions of informativeness.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials in the sample were tracked forward to assess the proportion attaining each informativeness condition.
source: Trials in our sample were then tracked forward to assess the proportion attaining each informativeness condition.

claim: 'Informative trials' were trials that fulfilled all four conditions of informativeness.
source: 'Informative trials' were trials that fulfilled all four conditions of informativeness.

source: Measures were chosen based on (i) close correspondence with each informativeness condition; (ii) objective and reproducible dichotomous scoring; and (iii) feasibility of assessment.

source: trial importance (determined by citation of reported trial results in high-quality clinical synthesizing documents; the premise of this surrogate is that these documents focus on questions of clinical importance)

claim: The premise of the trial importance surrogate is that high-quality clinical synthesizing documents focus on questions of clinical importance.
source: trial importance (determined by citation of reported trial results in high-quality clinical synthesizing documents; the premise of this surrogate is that these documents focus on questions of clinical importance)
evidence: This claim represents the authors' rationale for their methodological choice.

claim: Trial design quality was assessed using a modified Cochrane risk of bias tool, which is designed to identify threats to study internal validity.
source: trial design quality (assessed using a modified Cochrane ROB tool, which is designed to identify threats to study internal validity)
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

source: trial feasibility (established based on ability to achieve adequate participant enrollment and timely primary outcome completion)
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

source: and reporting (based on accessibility of primary outcome results via deposition on ClinicalTrials.gov or in journal publications).

source: We identified all trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov in our three disease areas with a start date from January 1, 2009 to December 31, 2010 inclusive (Supplementary file 8).

source: Our time range provided a minimum of 9 years of follow-up for maturation toward trial completion and fulfillment of all four surrogates of informativeness.

claim: Trials were downloaded from ClinicalTrials.gov on May 15, 2020.
source: Trials were downloaded from ClinicalTrials.gov on May 15, 2020.

source: We updated trial status and enrollment for all trials meeting our inclusion criteria on October 6, 2021.

claim: The study included randomized trials evaluating interventions of any type.
source: We included randomized trials (i) evaluating interventions of any type
evidence: This claim describes the inclusion criteria used in the study.

claim: The study included trials aimed at the treatment or prevention of ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, or lung cancer.
source: (ii) aimed at the treatment or prevention of ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, or lung cancer
evidence: This claim describes the inclusion criteria used in the study.

claim: The study included trials with at least one site in the United States (most of which will thus have a regulatory requirement for results reporting).
source: (iii) with at least one site in the United States (most of which will thus have a regulatory requirement for results reporting) (U.S. Public Law, 2007b)
evidence: This claim describes the inclusion criteria used in the study and provides a rationale based on regulatory requirements.

claim: The study included interventions that were FDA approved, that advanced to FDA approval, or interventions not subject to FDA approval (e.g. cardiac rehabilitation).
source: and (iv) interventions that were FDA approved, that advanced to FDA approval, or interventions not subject to FDA approval (e.g. cardiac rehabilitation).
evidence: This claim describes the inclusion criteria used in the study.

claim: The study excluded studies that exclusively evaluated safety, diagnostic, or screening interventions.
source: We did not include trials that we deemed unlikely to be targeted at informing clinical practice by excluding: (i) studies that exclusively evaluated safety, diagnostic, or screening interventions
evidence: This claim describes the exclusion criteria used in the study.

claim: The study excluded early phase trials (phase 0 or phase 1).
source: and (ii) early phase trials (phase 0 or phase 1) (Supplementary file 9; Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This claim describes the exclusion criteria used in the study.

claim: Phase 2 trials were included in the study as they are frequently used to inform both clinical and regulatory decision-making, particularly in cancer.
source: Phase 2 trials were included in our study as they are frequently used to inform both clinical and regulatory decision-making, particularly in cancer, where over one-quarter of recent FDA cancer drug approvals were based on the results of phase 1/2 or phase 2 clinical trials (Tibau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim represents the authors' rationale for including phase 2 trials, supported by a citation.

claim: Over one-quarter of recent FDA cancer drug approvals were based on the results of phase 1/2 or phase 2 clinical trials.
source: Phase 2 trials were included in our study as they are frequently used to inform both clinical and regulatory decision-making, particularly in cancer, where over one-quarter of recent FDA cancer drug approvals were based on the results of phase 1/2 or phase 2 clinical trials (Tibau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Trials were independently screened and assessed for eligibility by two authors (NH and HM), with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (JK).
source: Trials were independently screened and assessed for eligibility by two authors (NH and HM), with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (JK).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Two authors (NH and HM) independently scored all trials for the surrogate measures of the four conditions of informativeness.
source: Two authors (NH and HM) independently scored all trials for the surrogate measures of the four conditions of informativeness (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Disagreements in scoring were resolved by a third reviewer (JK).
source: Disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer (JK).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Conditions were scored sequentially because of their logical relationship among surrogate measures and workflow.
source: Because of their logical relationship among surrogate measures (e.g. citation in a high-quality clinical synthesizing documents cannot be assessed unless trial results are available) and workflow (e.g. ROB information is often available in SRs), conditions were scored sequentially.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' rationale for their methodological approach.

claim: Trials not meeting one condition were not advanced for evaluation of subsequent conditions.
source: Trials not meeting one condition were not advanced for evaluation of subsequent conditions.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The order of scoring was: (i) feasibility; (ii) reporting; (iii) importance; and (iv) design.
source: The order of scoring was as follows: (i) feasibility; (ii) reporting; (iii) importance; and (iv) design.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials meeting all four conditions were deemed informative; trials failing on any condition possessed features that compromised their informativeness.
source: Trials meeting all four conditions were deemed informative; trials failing on any condition possessed features that compromised their informativeness.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Completed trials were deemed to have not fulfilled feasibility if final participant enrollment was less than 85% of expected enrollment as listed in the final registration record prior to study start.
source: Completed trials were deemed to have not fulfilled feasibility if final participant enrollment was less than 85% of expected enrollment as listed in the final registration record prior to study start, thus reflecting a substantial loss of statistical power for the primary outcome (Carlisle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study, with a citation supporting the rationale.

claim: Enrollment less than 85% of expected enrollment reflects a substantial loss of statistical power for the primary outcome.
source: Completed trials were deemed to have not fulfilled feasibility if final participant enrollment was less than 85% of expected enrollment as listed in the final registration record prior to study start, thus reflecting a substantial loss of statistical power for the primary outcome (Carlisle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about the impact of under-enrollment.

claim: Terminated trials were deemed infeasible if the reason for termination in the ClinicalTrials.gov registration record involved accrual, feasibility, funding, or another non-scientific reason.
source: Terminated trials were deemed infeasible if the reason for termination in the ClinicalTrials.gov registration record involved accrual, feasibility, funding, or another non-scientific reason (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials terminated for scientific reasons (accumulated scientific data suggesting early efficacy, futility, or toxicity) were deemed feasible irrespective of the proportion of expected enrollment achieved.
source: Trials terminated for scientific reasons (accumulated scientific data suggesting early efficacy, futility, or toxicity) were deemed feasible irrespective of the proportion of expected enrollment achieved.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials that were ongoing were categorized as infeasible if they had already surpassed double the intended time for primary completion.
source: Trials that were ongoing were categorized as infeasible if they had already surpassed double the intended time for primary completion, which was calculated by subtracting the intended primary completion date (as stated in the final registration record prior to study start) from the trial start date, then multiplying by 2.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Interventional clinical trials of FDA-regulated drug, biologic, or device interventions are subject to trial registration and results submission requirements outlined in Section 801 of the Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act (FDAAA 801).
source: Interventional clinical trials of FDA-regulated drug, biologic, or device interventions are subject to trial registration and results submission requirements outlined in Section 801 of the Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act (FDAAA 801) (U.S. Public Law, 2007a).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about regulatory requirements, supported by a citation.

claim: Other types of trials are encouraged to register based on policies such as the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) requirement for public registration, but will fall outside the scope of FDAAA 801 results submission requirements.
source: Other types of trials, also contained in our cohort, are encouraged to register based on policies such as the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) requirement for public registration (De Angelis et al., 2004), but will fall outside the scope of FDAAA 801 results submission requirements.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about registration policies, supported by a citation.

claim: Trials were categorized as reported if they either had primary outcome results available on ClinicalTrials.gov or in a publication.
source: Trials were categorized as reported if they either had primary outcome results available on ClinicalTrials.gov or in a publication (Supplementary file 13).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: When more than one publication presented primary outcome results, the earliest published report was identified and advanced to the next step of assessment.
source: When more than one publication presented primary outcome results, the earliest published report was identified and advanced to the next step of assessment.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: ClinicalTrials.gov results reporting and publication search were updated in October 2021 for those trials previously deemed to have not met the criteria for reporting.
source: ClinicalTrials.gov results reporting and publication search were updated in October 2021 for those trials previously deemed to have not met the criteria for reporting.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Importance was scored by determining whether trial results were included in a high-quality review document designed to inform medical decision-making.
source: Importance was scored by determining whether trial results were included in a high-quality review document designed to inform medical decision-making.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials were first assessed for inclusion in the results of a high-quality systematic review to credit trials with being informative even if they produced negative results, given that systematic review citation practices are results neutral.
source: To credit trials with being informative even if they produced negative results, trials were first assessed for inclusion in the results of a high-quality SR, given that SR citation practices are results neutral.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' rationale for their methodological approach.

claim: The study assessed for trial results citation in a Cochrane systematic review, Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality systematic review, or in a systematic review deemed of high quality based on a modified AMSTAR score.
source: We assessed for trial results citation in a Cochrane SR, Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality SR, or in an SR deemed of high quality based on a modified A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews (AMSTAR) score (Supplementary file 14).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials not cited in the results of high-quality systematic reviews were evaluated for inclusion in a high-quality clinical practice guideline.
source: Trials not cited in the results of high-quality SRs were evaluated for inclusion in a high-quality clinical practice guideline (CPG)
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials not cited in high-quality systematic reviews or clinical practice guidelines were then assessed for inclusion in an UpToDate review article.
source: remaining uncited trials were then assessed for inclusion in an UpToDate review article (Kluwer Logo, 2022; Supplementary file 15).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials cited in high-quality review documents were deemed to have fulfilled the importance condition.
source: Trials cited in high-quality review documents were deemed to have fulfilled the importance condition.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Assessment of importance was updated in October 2021 for all trials previously deemed to have not met the criterion for importance.
source: Assessment of importance was updated in October 2021 for all trials previously deemed to have not met the criterion for importance.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Design was assessed by determining whether studies were at elevated risk of bias, using a modified Cochrane risk of bias tool.
source: Finally, design was assessed by determining whether studies were at elevated ROB, using a modified Cochrane ROB tool (Higgins et al., 2011; Supplementary file 16).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: When available, risk of bias scores were extracted directly from the most recent high-quality systematic review identified during the assessment of trial importance.
source: When available, ROB scores were extracted directly from the most recent high-quality SR identified during the assessment of trial importance.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: When risk of bias scores were unavailable, they were independently performed by two authors (NH and HM), with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (JK).
source: When unavailable, ROB scores were independently performed by two authors (NH and HM), with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer (JK).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Information from both the primary study publication and the ClinicalTrials.gov registration record was used in risk of bias assessments.
source: Information from both the primary study publication and the ClinicalTrials.gov registration record was used in our ROB assessments.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Trials were deemed to have fulfilled the design condition of informativeness if all risk of bias elements were deemed to be of low risk of bias, or a majority were of low risk of bias with a minority of elements deemed to be of unclear risk of bias.
source: Trials were deemed to have fulfilled the design condition of informativeness if all ROB elements were deemed to be of low ROB, or a majority were of low ROB with a minority of elements deemed to be of unclear ROB.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study provided a 95% binomial confidence interval for the primary outcome.
source: We provided a 95% binomial CI for our primary outcome.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study performed a sensitivity analysis on the primary outcome excluding small, pilot-type studies identified based on an anticipated participant enrollment below the lowest quartile of target enrollment for the cohort of trials.
source: We performed a sensitivity analysis on our primary outcome excluding small, pilot-type studies that would not have been designed to inform clinical decision-making. These were identified based on an anticipated participant enrollment below the lowest quartile of target enrollment for our cohort of trials.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study performed a second sensitivity analysis on the primary outcome excluding Phase 1/2 and phase 2 trials due to concern that Phase 2 trials are less likely to inform clinical practice than trials of a higher phase.
source: Due to concern that Phase 2 trials are less likely to inform clinical practice than trials of a higher phase, we performed a second sensitivity analysis on our primary outcome excluding Phase 1/2 and phase 2 trials.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study and the rationale for it.

claim: As secondary outcomes, the study estimated the proportion of trial participants who were enrolled in informative trials.
source: As secondary outcomes, we estimated the proportion of trial participants who were enrolled in informative trials.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study reported the proportion of informative trials in each of the three disease areas and the proportion of trials advancing across each condition of informativeness.
source: We also report the proportion of informative trials in each of our three disease areas and the proportion of trials advancing across each condition of informativeness.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study provided 95% binomial confidence intervals for the proportion of informative trials in each disease area and the proportion of trials advancing across each condition of informativeness.
source: We provided 95% binomial CI for the latter two secondary outcomes.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study compared the proportion of informative trials between disease categories and by trial sponsor using the Chi-square test and provided binomial confidence intervals for each stratum.
source: We compared the proportion of informative trials between disease categories and by trial sponsor using the Chi-square test (chisq.test function in R) and provided binomial CI for each stratum.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study used the fisher.test function in R to perform a two-sided Fisher's exact test assessing the proportion of informative trials by type of intervention and trial phase and provided exact confidence intervals for each.
source: We used the fisher.test function in R to perform a two-sided Fisher's exact test assessing the proportion of informative trials by type of intervention and trial phase and provided exact CI for each.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study calculated inter-rater agreement rates using Cohen's kappa.
source: We calculated inter-rater agreement rates using Cohen's kappa (Supplementary file 17).
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: The study defined p<0.05 as statistically significant.
source: We defined p<0.05 as statistically significant.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis used in the study.

claim: All analyses were performed using R version 4.0.2.
source: All analyses were performed using R version 4.0.2. (R Development Core Team, 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the statistical software used in the study.

source: Our study was not subject to Institutional Review Board approval, as it relied on publicly accessible data.

source: The study protocol was prospectively registered on Open Science Framework (Hutchinson et al., 2020)

source: deviations and amendments to the study protocol are detailed in Supplementary file 18.
evidence: This claim describes where protocol deviations are documented.

source: The code (Hutchinson N, 2022) and data set Hutchinson et al., 2020 used in this analysis are available online.

claim: This study follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guidelines for cohort studies.
source: This study follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guidelines for cohort studies (Supplementary file 19).
